entry.title: TicketTak - Kenolab
entry.content:
TicketTak is a two-host Active Directory chain from Kenolab built around Kerberos ticket abuse. I’ll start with a web-based availability checker that fetches internal URLs, one of which has no DNS record. Any domain user can write to ADIDNS, so I’ll claim that name, point it at my host, and relay the machine account’s HTTP authentication to LDAP to write shadow credentials onto the computer object. From there a PKINIT certificate gets me a TGT for the machine account, and S4U2self turns that into a ticket for administrator on the host itself. On that box is an Ansible inventory with a vault-encrypted password that cracks to a domain user, who can read an IT share holding a previous pentest report. The report pastes the krbtgt AES key, so I’ll forge a golden ticket for the domain.

Recon

nmap

On the first host, the mix of DNS, Kerberos, LDAP, and SMB says domain controller

The second host has a webserver on port 80

Both are Windows Server 2022 Build 20348, with hostnames DC01 and WEB01

I’ll use netexec to generate the hosts file for me

There’s one thing to keep in mind. SMB signing on WEB01 is disabled, which marks it as a relay target

SMB

The provided creds work on the DC and it has three non-default shares. IT, MGMT, and RH all look interesting, but the pentest user has no access to any of them

We can list the domain users; the list is small

BloodHound

I’ll collect bloodhound data with bloodhound-python

There’s nothing to abuse in bloodhound. The pentest user has no interesting ACLs

Port 80

Port 80 on WEB01 is an app called KenoMonitor “Internal Web Availability Checker”. The server fetches whichever target is picked. If we try to submit “example.com” we get “Unknow host”, so the box has no route out. There are two other internal names and neither resolves:

WEB01

Strategy

We can point git.kenocorp.lan to our host (ADIDNS) and trigger a check, so WEB01 authenticates to us over HTTP as the machine account. Then we can relay that authentication to LDAP on the DC. A computer object can write its own msDS-KeyCredentialLink, so the relay can plant shadow credentials on WEB01$. Finally, we can use the resulting certificate for PKINIT to get a TGT as WEB01$, then use S4U2self to get a ticket for administrator on WEB01.

ADIDNS

We can use dnstool.py from krbrelayx to add the record:

The record takes a couple of minutes to resolve. Eventually it does:

Shadow Credentials

I’ll start ntlmrelayx.py listening on port 80, relaying to LDAP on the DC, with the shadow credentials attack pointed at WEB01$

Now I’ll run the check against git.kenocorp.lan. The relay then gets what it needs

The certificate is written and WEB01$ now trusts the matching key. Now let’s run the command it told us to run to get TGT for WEB01$

S4U2self

A machine account can always ask the KDC for a ticket to itself on behalf of any user (S4U2self abuse), even with no delegation configured. That’s enough to get a service ticket for administrator to WEB01:

The ticket authenticates as administrator on WEB01 and we can grab the user flag

Auth as pierre.durand

Enumeration

There’s a non-standard directory at the root of C:, C:\OPS

The Ansible inventory has a WinRM password for pierre.durand, encrypted with ansible-vault:

Crack Vault

A vault blob is PBKDF2-SHA256, which john handles. I’ll save the blob and convert it:

Now we can decrypt the vault using this password

The creds are good, and pierre.durand can read the IT share

Shell as Administrator on DC01

IT Share

There are some documents in the Security folder inside the IT share

pentest_report.pdf is a report from a previous engagement, and the persistence section pastes the full secretsdump.py output for krbtgt as a proof. The report masked the administrator password but left the krbtgt keys in full. The AES256 key is a7977840e57a5e7dcf400ee05b0617e8e90c3b5b3828e86505a0d15c0f51ea59

Golden Ticket

Forging a golden ticket needs the domain SID as well:

The krbtgt password has not been rotated since the report, so the key still signs valid tickets:

The ticket works against the DC:

Let’s grab the root flag
entry.summary: ADIDNS spoofing, NTLM relay to shadow credentials, S4U2self, Ansible Vault, golden ticket

entry.title: GameMaster - Kenolab
entry.content:
Gamemaster is an easy Active Directory machine from Kenolab (https://www.kenolab.eu/welcome), created by Anh4ckin and PhoeniX. It involves SQLi, user enumeration, AS-REP roasting with Kerberoasting to get a crackable hash for a service account, ACL abuse and decrypting an RDG file to get the administrator password.

Recon

nmap

We start with a full port scan

The open ports show we are dealing with a Domain Controller: DNS (53), Kerberos (88), LDAP (389/636), SMB (445) and WinRM (5985/5986). There is also a web server on port 80, worth a closer look.

I’ll use netexec to generate the hosts file line and add it to /etc/hosts

SMB

Since we don’t have any credentials yet, we can start by trying to list the SMB shares using null and guest authentication. Both are disabled in this case

Port 80

There’s a website on port 80 with a /backups folder, but access to it is forbidden. The /search.asp page looks like a good target for SQL injection so let’s run sqlmap against it

Backup file

Thankfully, that wasn’t complicated, and sqlmap managed to dump the whole database. Nothing looked interesting, like credentials or password hashes, but one thing stood out: a backup file at /backups/backup_20260126-oldsite-frontend.bak. We can try to access it directly with the full url: http://10.253.163.14/backups/backup_20260126-oldsite-frontend.bak. Let’s download it locally

It’s a zip archive containing several pdf files. Nothing looked interesting in them, as they were all dummy text

Auth as iis_svc

User enumeration

One useful thing we can pull from those PDFs is the author field, which holds several names we can parse into usernames

Since we don’t know the username format, we can use username-anarchy. It takes a list of names in first last format and generates many common username formats, which we can then test with a tool like kerbrute to see which ones are valid

Running kerbrute against the dc with the generated usernames file returned 5 valid users

Let’s save these usernames into a file

AS-REP roasting

Now that we have valid usernames, we can try AS-REP roasting to see if any of them are vulnerable

Nice! We got the hash of marc.shadow, so let’s try to crack it with john. Unfortunately, it doesn’t crack

Kerberoasting through AS-REQ

Another thing we can try is this research from Semperis, which shows that an account with DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH set can be abused to kerberoast other users. We can do this easily with netexec using the --no-preauth-targets flag

It dumped the hash of the iis_svc user, and this time the hash cracked with john

Shell as lucas.morau

BloodHound

With valid credentials in hand, we can run BloodHound to gain a better understanding of the network and the permissions our users have

Looking at BloodHound, we can see that iis_svc has GenericAll over the IT OU

OU ACL abuse

GenericAll on the OU gives us control of the OU object itself, but not automatically of the objects inside it. To get that, we use Impacket’s dacledit to add an inheritable FullControl ACE for iis_svc (the -inheritance flag), so the rights propagate to the users and groups in the OU.

Back in BloodHound, the IT OU contains the Remote_Access group, and lucas.morau is a member of it. Since we granted ourselves FullControl on the OU with an inheritable ACE, that control should propagate to the objects inside it, including lucas.morau.

We can verify this with bloodyAD get writable, which lists every object we can modify. The output confirms we now have write access over lucas.morau, including DACL: WRITE and OWNER: WRITE, which effectively means full control of the account.

lucas.morau is the only user in the OU besides iis_svc that shows up with DACL: WRITE and OWNER: WRITE. The other users are missing, so let’s find out why by listing the OU’s users with their adminCount and group membership:

Every other user in the OU has adminCount: 1. These are protected accounts (members of privileged groups). They don’t inherit ACEs from their parent OU, which is why the dacledit warning mentioned adminCount=1. lucas.morau and iis_svc are the only ones without it, which makes lucas.morau our target: he is in Remote_Access, which should give us WinRM access.

Password reset

Let’s use bloodyAD to change lucas.morau’s password. GenericAll allows other approaches too (shadow credentials, for example), but I’m lazy and this is the quickest :)

Now let’s connect over WinRM with winrmexec and grab the user flag.

Shell as Administrator

RDCMan file

On the desktop there is a node13.rdg file. This is a Remote Desktop Connection Manager (RDCMan) configuration file that stores saved RDP connections, including usernames and DPAPI-encrypted passwords.

DPAPI decryption

The .rdg file stores its saved password as a DPAPI-encrypted blob. DPAPI ties the encryption key to the user who created it, and Windows makes that key available to any process running as that user. Since we are running as lucas.morau, who owns the file, we can decrypt the blob directly from our PowerShell session with ProtectedData.Unprotect and the CurrentUser scope, with no extra tooling and no need to know his password. This reveals the administrator’s password.

Let’s connect again with winrmexec, this time as the administrator, and grab the root flag.
entry.summary: SQLi, AS-REP roasting into Kerberoasting, OU ACL abuse, RDCMan password decryption

entry.title: AKTIVKATALOG 2 - Hack.lu CTF 2025
entry.content:
AKTIVKATALOG 2 is an Active Directory challenge from Hack.lu CTF 2025, created by NeffIsBack and Steffen. It involves Relaying, RBCD, and ACLs

Enumeration

I’ll use netexec to generate the hosts file line and add it to /etc/hosts

Let’s start by listing users using null authentication, surprisingly, it worked on the DC and gave us a list of users. One of them had their password in the description field

ta_bort.mig:LjtLNg37LdcZin73

The creds above do work

We can also try listing shares, but all are default in this case

Bloodhound

With valid credentials in hand, we can run Bloodhound to gain a better understanding of the network and the permissions our users have

However, our current user can’t do much

LDAP Signing & Channel Binding

We notice something very important here: there’s no LDAP signing or channel binding on the DC, this means NTLM authentication can be relayed. To learn more about this topic I suggest you read this blogpost from TrustedSec. More resources are listed in the resources section at the end of this writeup

Plan

The first thing we’ll do is coerce the authentication from SRV02, which is running the WebClient service. This will use the SRV02$ machine account to authenticate to our machine. Since WebDAV uses HTTP, the machine will authenticate using NTLM and because it’s a web request, we’ll be able to relay the authentication to LDAP, as signing isn’t enforced.

The relay will let us write the msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute on the target object then impersonate any user on the machine

NTLM Relay to LDAPS

We can use the webdav module from netexec to check if the WebClient Service is enabled on SRV02, which is the case here

We also check the Machine Account Quota value using the maq module

As you can see, the MachineAccountQuota value is 10, which is the default. This will let us create a machine account later for our RBCD attack, since each machine account comes with an SPN.

The only thing left now is to add a new DNS record that points to our attacker machine, because the WebClient connection string needs to be a hostname, not an IP address. This is something that’s allowed by default for all domain users.

Let’s use the dnstool.py tool from the krbrelayx repo

Let’s verify that the DNS record has been created and is pointing to our attacker’s IP address

Alternatively, we can use dnstool’s query parameter

Next, we setup our listener for relaying the authentication to LDAP on the DC with the --delegate-access flag to write the msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute on SRV02

It’s also possible to relay to LDAP

Finally, we can use dementor (or any similar like PetitPotam,…) to coerce Webclient HTTP authentication

Nice! the LDAP relay was successful, and ntlmrelayx.py created a machine account for us to delegate to SRV02

We can now request a service ticket as Administrator on SRV02

Or we can automate all of that using the --delegate option from netexec

SRV02 Post Exploitation

DPAPI

Let’s use the administratör account to look for DPAPI using the --dpapi flag from netexec

Nice! it dumped the password of the user maja.lindgren

DC01 Takeover

Looking at bloodhound, we can see that this user has some interesting permissions

  • maja.lindgren has AddMember over KONTOANSVARIGA group
  • KONTOANSVARIGA has AllExtendedRights over DC01

That’s a nice path to pwn the DC :)

First, let’s add our user to the KONTOANSVARIGA group using BloodyAD

Now that we have the AllExtendedRights privilege over the DC, we can just change the DC01$ account password and perform a DCSync

Finally, we can grab our flag

That concludes this challenge. I hope you learned something new! 🐱

Resources

  • https://trustedsec.com/blog/a-comprehensive-guide-on-relaying-anno-2022
  • https://logan-goins.com/2024-07-23-ldap-relay/
entry.summary: NTLM relay, RBCD, and ACLs

entry.title: AKTIVKATALOG 1 - Hack.lu CTF 2025
entry.content:
AKTIVKATALOG 1 is an Active Directory challenge from Hack.lu CTF 2025, created by NeffIsBack and Steffen. It involves enumerating the unixUserPassword attribute and ADCS

Note

My NetExec version is the latest, I installed it using:

My Certipy version is:

Enumeration

I’ll use netexec to generate the hosts file line and add it to /etc/hosts

Running netexec with the --users and --shares flags doesn’t show anything suspicious. However, we can use the --computers flag to enumerate domain computers

As you can see, we have the DC01$ account and another computer account called dator$. There’s an LDAP attribute called unixUserPassword that is sometimes populated with plaintext credentials. To enumerate it, we can use the get-unixUserPassword module from netexec, which in this case returns the computer account’s password

Now that we have credentials, we can do further enumeration like listing users and shares but nothing is interesting was found

ADCS

One important thing to check in an Active Directory environment is ADCS (Active Directory Certificate Services). Let’s use the adcs module from netexec to see if it’s in use

Indeed, ADCS is present here. The next step is to look for vulnerable templates using tools like Certipy. Netexec recently added a new module called certipy-find that works like the certipy find command to look for vulnerable templates

We can also do the same thing using certipy

As you can see from the output of both tools, the köttbullar template is vulnerable to ESC1 and ESC15. In this writeup we will exploit both

ESC1

certipy wiki is a nice place to find more information about ESC1 and the commands to exploit it. I also created a cheatsheet for ADCS that includes all the commands to exploit each escalation. More ADCS resources are listed in the resources section at the end of this writeup

With the Domain Administrator hash in hand, we can grab our flag located in C:\Users\Administratör\Desktop\flag.txt

ESC15

We will exploit Scenario A which is Direct Impersonation via Schannel (Injecting "Client Authentication" Application Policy)

With this ldap shell we can do a lot. The easiest way is to create a new user and add them to the domain admins (sorry I mean Domänadministratörer) group

Now we can grab our flag, just like before

That concludes this challenge. I hope you learned something new! 🐱

Resources

  • https://www.netexec.wiki/
  • https://github.com/ly4k/Certipy/wiki/06-%E2%80%90-Privilege-Escalation
  • https://xbz0n.sh/blog/adcs-complete-attack-reference
  • https://logan-goins.com/2024-05-04-ADCS/
  • https://seriotonctf.github.io/ADCS-Attacks-with-Certipy/

entry.title: Pwning Reflection Using NTLM Reflection
entry.content:
This post only demonstrates the attack. For a detailed writeup on the “Reflection” chain, I’ve already created one, which you can find here: https://seriotonctf.github.io/Reflection-Vulnlab/

Recently, Synacktiv published a blog post about CVE-2025-33073, an NTLM Reflection attack. In this post, I’ll demonstrate how this vulnerability can be leveraged in the “Reflection” chain from Vulnlab. For an in-depth analysis, refer to the original blog post by Synacktiv

Conditions

For this attack to succeed, the following conditions must be met:

  • SMB signing must be disabled on the target
  • The attacker must have permission to create DNS records

Attack

First, we need to check whether our targets have SMB signing disabled or not

netexec confirms that SMB signing is not enforced (signing:False) on all three target machines, making them potentially vulnerable to this attack

Registering a DNS Record

We need to register a new DNS record, in this case localhost1UWhRCAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAwbEAYBAAAA and make it point to our IP address

Alternatively, we can create a new DNS record using the hostname of the machine we want to exploit, for example, DC01

Let’s verify that the DNS record has been created and is pointing to our attacker’s IP address

Alternatively, we can use the dig command

Coercion

Now, we just need to coerce authentication to the DNS record we previously created


We can also use the coerce_plus module from Netexec

Attack Worked

As you can see, the attack was successful, and we were able to perform a SAM dump because the SYSTEM token was used for authentication

In the same way, we can target MS01 and WS01

MS01

WS01

entry.title: Shibuya - Vulnlab
entry.content:
Shibuya is a medium-difficulty Active Directory machine on VulnLab, created by xct. It involves user enumeration, SMB shares, cross-session relay attack, and ESC1

User

Nmap

From the Nmap scan, we can see that we’re dealing with a Domain Controller, as it has DNS and Kerberos services running. Additionally, SSH is open, which is unusual

SMB

We can try listing shares using null authentication and guest authentication, but in this case, both failed

We don’t have any valid credentials either, so let’s try to enumerate users using kerbrute with the xato-net-10-million-usernames wordlist

In this case, we got two users: purple and red (this is a Jujutsu Kaisen reference, just like the name of the machine)
We don’t have a password yet, but we can try using the username as the password, sometimes this works

Using NTLM authentication doesn’t work; however, when we add -k to authenticate using Kerberos, it works

Awesome! Now that we have valid credentials, we can enumerate further. Running --shares to look for SMB shares, we notice two non-standard shares called users and images$, but we only have read access to the users share

Let’s get a ticket and connect to the users share using smbclient from impacket

As you can see, we have more users that we can add to our users file. We can also try accessing each folder, but in this case, we get a permission denied

Let’s also enumerate more domain users using the --users flag in NetExec

In this case, we get a lot of users, but one of them stands out, svc_autojoin has what looks like a password in his description

We can check if this user can access the images$ share we saw earlier, and indeed, he can

After connecting and listing the files, we see some .wim files, which stand for Windows Imaging Format. It’s a disk image file format that contains a snapshot of a Windows installation

Let’s download them to our local machine and take a look

We can mount those files, but a simpler way is to run 7z on them to extract the contents

We have the home directories of Administrator and simon.watson, but there’s nothing interesting there. Let’s move on to the second WIM file and repeat the same process we used on the first one.

Nice! There are the SAM, SYSTEM, and SECURITY hives. Let’s dump them using secretsdump from impacket

Awesome, we got some hashes. You’d think it’s the Administrator’s hash, but it’s not. We can try spraying the Administrator and Operator user hashes with the list of users we got earlier, but in this case, it’s reasonable to guess that the Operator hash belongs to the simon.watson user, since he’s the one present on the machine, as we saw from the first WIM file we extracted

Remember earlier, we couldn’t cd into Simon’s folder. Now that we have his credentials, we can connect to the users’ share and list his home directory

We can get the user flag from the desktop

Now we need a way to get a shell on the box. Remember from the Nmap scan that SSH is open. Let’s create a .ssh folder inside the user’s home directory and place our key there

And we’re in!

Another way we can connect to SSH is by using changepasswd from Impacket to change Simon’s password using his hash, since we can’t use pass-the-hash with SSH

ROOT

Since LDAP is closed, we weren’t able to gather BloodHound data earlier. But now that we have an SSH connection, we can open a SOCKS proxy and use it to collect BloodHound data remotely with NetExec

The next step is tricky to find. If we run ps to list running processes, we can see that Explorer is running, so it looks like someone is logged in

We can try to list more information about the session using the qwinsta command, but in this case, it failed

Somehow, if we run it with runas it works, as shown here

As you can see, the user nigel.mills has a session with an ID of 1. Another way to enumerate this is by checking the “Sessions” option in BloodHound, it should show that the user nigel has a session on the DC

Cross Session Relay

With this information in hand, we can perform a cross-session relay attack (that’s why the machine is called Shibuya) and capture Nigel’s hash. You can refer to 0xdf’s write-up on Rebound here.
To carry out the attack we need to download the RemotePotato0 binary and upload it to the target machine. The attack can also be performed using KrbRelay, but I prefer the first option
First, we run socat like this

Then, we execute RemotePotato0 on the target machine

And as you can see, we’ve captured nigel’s hash. Let’s save it to a file and crack it with john

ADCS

Let’s look for vulnerable templates using certipy

Since nigel.mills is a member of the t1_admins group we can exploit this easily

ESC1

Here we use the _admin upn because he’s the domain admin

Nice! we got the pfx, now we can use it to get his hash

But we got an error saying [-] Object SID mismatch between certificate and user '_admin'. This is intended actually, earlier this February, Microsoft started enforcing the SID: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/topic/kb5014754-certificate-based-authentication-changes-on-windows-domain-controllers-ad2c23b0-15d8-4340-a468-4d4f3b188f16

By February 2025, if the StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement registry key is not configured, domain controllers will move to Full Enforcement mode

However, we can just set the SID in the request

With the DA hash in hand, we can perform a DCSync, but I’ll just read the flag via SMB

Beyond root

Pre-Created Computer Accounts

The red:red and purple:purple worked because both are precreated machine accounts. We can verify by running the pre2k module in NetExec

Exploiting ESC3

I don’t think I covered how to exploit ESC3 in my blog, so this is a great opportunity to demonstrate it

That concludes this machine. I hope you learned something new! 🐱

Resources

  • https://security.stackexchange.com/questions/272327/cannot-qwinsta-during-winrm-but-it-works-when-run-under-newcredentials-logo
  • https://0xdf.gitlab.io/2024/03/30/htb-rebound.html#cross-session-relay
  • https://github.com/antonioCoco/RemotePotato0
  • https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/topic/kb5014754-certificate-based-authentication-changes-on-windows-domain-controllers-ad2c23b0-15d8-4340-a468-4d4f3b188f16
  • https://trustedsec.com/blog/diving-into-pre-created-computer-accounts
entry.summary: active directory, cross-session relay, esc1

entry.title: HTB: Solving Cicada Using Only NetExec
entry.content:
This post simply demonstrates how to solve the machine using only NetExec. For a more in-depth walkthrough, check out ippsec’s video and 0xdf’s writeup

Cicada is an easy Active Directory machine from HackTheBox. The core concepts here are users enumeration, password spraying, SMB shares and Backup Operators group. In this writeup, I will walk through the entire machine using only NetExec.

Make sure you have the latest version of Netexec by upgrading it with pipx using the following command

USER

Enumeration

First, we use the --generate-hosts-file option, which automatically retrieves the domain name and netbios name, then generates an entry we can add to our /etc/hosts file

SMB

Let’s attempt guest authentication by using any username and password. As you can see, we are able to list shares with guest access. There are non-default shares named “HR” and “DEV”, let’s take note of them

Now, let’s use the --rid-brute option to enumerate domain users

We can clean up the output to get a nice list of users

Another thing we can try is the spider_plus module, which searches file shares with read access

The spider_plus module saves the list of files in a json file. In our case, it dumped the results in “/tmp/nxc_hosted/nxc_spider_plus/10.10.11.35.json”. Looking at the output, we can see a file inside the HR share called “Notice from HR.txt”, which we have read access to

We can use the --get-file option along with the --share option to grab the file to our local machine

Inspecting the file reveals a plaintext password

Since we dont know which user that password belongs to, we can spray it with the list of users we gathered earlier. In this case, we get a hit for the user “michael.wrightson”

With these credentials in hand, we can use the --users flag to enumerate more users and check their descriptions, as some users may store their passwords there

Or, we can use the get-desc-users module for ldap, which only retrieves the descriptions of the users

We can see a note in david.orelious’ description revealing his password

Let’s check if our new user has access to the DEV share using the --shares option

Indeed, the user has read access to that share. Once again, let’s use the spider_plus module to look for interesting files

There’s a PowerShell script called “Backup_script.ps1” inside the share

We can use the same command as before to download the PowerShell script from the DEV share

Looking through the script, we find hardcoded credentials for the user emily.oscars

These credentials are valid for SMB

They also work for winrm and we can PsRemote (Pwn3d!)

I can’t use Evil-WinRM here to grab the flag since I’m only using NetExec for this walkthrough… oh wait, NetExec has an option to execute PowerShell commands remotely using the -X option—so I can grab the flag anyway!

Root

Let’s start by checking which groups our user belongs to using the groupmembership module for LDAP

Looking at the output, we see that our user is a member of the Backup Operators group, a high-privilege group. This allows us to dump NTDS

Backup Operators

Recently, @mpgn_x64 (https://x.com/mpgn_x64) added a new module to Netexec called backup_operator which is a very neat addition! Thanks for that

This module handles everything for us and dumps the Administrator hash. We can use this hash to login to the box and read the root flag

In fact, why even bother logging into the box when we can just grab the flag directly with -x? (Thanks to Pwn3d! 😎)

Resources

  • https://www.netexec.wiki/
  • https://x.com/mpgn_x64
  • https://x.com/mpgn_x64/status/1878899208465600756
  • https://www.thehacker.recipes/ad/movement/builtins/security-groups#practice
  • https://www.thehacker.recipes/ad/movement/credentials/dumping/sam-and-lsa-secrets
  • https://github.com/seriotonctf/cme-nxc-cheat-sheet

entry.title: Redelegate - Vulnlab
entry.content:
Redelegate is a hard Active Directory machine from Vulnlab, created by Geiseric. It involves enumerating domain accounts via MSSQL, abusing GenericAll on a machine account, and performing constrained delegation.

User

Enumeration

NMAP

From the Nmap scan, we can see that we are dealing with a Domain Controller, as it has DNS, LDAP, and Kerberos services running. Additionally, there is FTP on port 21 an MSSQL service running on port 1433, which is particularly noteworthy

FTP

We can connect to FTP anonymously and list files

Let’s switch to binary mode, disable the prompt, and download all the files

In the files, they mentioned weak passwords like the “SeasonYear!” format and outlined ongoing issues with unused Active Directory objects and dangerous ACLs.

We can use this format to create a wordlist to use for password spraying

Currently, We don’t have any valid users to test these passwords with, but remember that one of the files we retrieved from FTP is a Keepass database

We can attempt to crack this file with john by providing the wordlist we created

Now, we can use export the content of the database using keepassxc-cli

Great, now we have a list of usernames and passwords. One username in particular stands out: the sqlguest account. We can try it with MSSQL

MSSQL

We managed to log in, but it’s just a guest account. The first thing I always do is run xp_dirtree to capture the hash of the account running the SQL service.

We obtained the hash of the sql_svc account, but it could not be cracked.
At this point, it seemed like a dead end. However, after some research, we found this blogpost from 2015, which describes a method to enumerate domain users using MSSQL.

Enumerating Domain Accounts

The steps to achieve this are outlined in the blog post. The first step is to retrieve the domain name.

Next, we use a default group, in this case, Domain Admins, to retrieve the RID

Once the full RID has been obtained, we can extract the domain SID by taking the first 48 bytes. In our case, it’s 0x010500000000000515000000A185DEEFB22433798D8E847AF4010000. We can use the following python code to convert the SID to a readable format

Refer to steps 6 through 12 in the Manual Process for Enumerating Domain Accounts section of the blog post.

After obtaining the SID, we can start generating our own RIDs and begin fuzzing

This script will generate a file like this

Each line represents a query for a specific RID appended to the base SID. We can pass this file to mssqlclient.py using the -file option and let it enumerate and print all the domain users

After some time, we end up with a comprehensive list of usernames and groups.

With some cleanup, we can extract a list of just the user accounts

Foothold

Now that we have the domain users, we can perform a password spray using the wordlist we created earlier

We successfully got a hit on the user Marie.Curie. Let’s gather Bloodhound data to gain a better understanding of the network and the permissions our user have

ForceChangePassword

After loading the data into BloodHound, we identified 10 Reachable High Value Targets from our current user, Marie.Curie.

She is a member of the Helpdesk group, which has the ForceChangePassword permission on the user Helen.Frost. We can use bloodyAD to change Helen’s password

Now, we can use evil-winrm to access the filesystem and grab our user flag

Privilege Escalation

Running whoami /priv reveals that our user has the SeEnableDelegationPrivilege, a dangerous permission that allows for both constrained and unconstrained delegations

A word on Delegation

There are 3 types of delegation:

  • Unconstrained delegations (KUD): a service can impersonate users on any other service.
  • Constrained delegations (KCD): a service can impersonate users on a set of services
  • Resource based constrained delegations (RBCD) : a set of services can impersonate users on a service

I’ll leave some resources to learn more about delegation in the Resources section below

Constrained Delegation

GenericAll

Since we can’t add DNS entries and maq is set to 0, our only option is Constrained Delegation. However, Constrained Delegation requires a machine account, and fortunately, our user Helen.Frost has GenericAll over FS01$, which allows us to change its password.

Now that we have full control over FS01$, we can use it to execute the Constrained Delegation attack.
As mentioned in this blogpost to perform Constrained Delegation, the following steps are required:

  • The userAccountControl attribute for the object must be updated with the TRUSTED_TO_AUTHENTICATE_FOR_DELEGATION flag.
  • The msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo attribute must be populated with the SPN configured on the delegation tab

To proceed, let’s first set msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo to cifs (or ldap)

Next, let’s set the TrustedToAuthForDelegation flag

To confirm that the attributes have been successfully set, we can use findDelegation from Impacket

Another way to set the TrustedToAuthForDelegation is to use bloodyAD

Now, we use the credentials of fs01 to request a service ticket while impersonating any user.

Notice that we cannot impersonate the Administrator user in this case because it has the NOT_DELEGATED attribute, meaning it’s a protected account, as you can see here

However, we can impersonate ryan.cooper since he is a Domain Admin

As you can see, we successfully authenticated using the ticket

DCSync

Next, let’s perform a DCSync attack and dump all the hashes, even though we can simply connect as ryan.cooper and retrieve the root flag

That concludes this machine. I hope you learned something new! 🐱

entry.title: Retro2 - Vulnlab
entry.content:
Introduction

Retro2 is an easy Active Directory box from Vulnlab that involves decrypting an MS Access database, Pre-Created Computer Accounts, GenericWrite, AddMember and finally exploiting an RpcEptMapper Registry Key vulnerability in Windows 7 / Server 2008 R2.

NMAP

From the Nmap scan, we can see that we are dealing with a Domain Controller, as indicated by the presence of DNS, Kerberos and LDAP.

Enumeration

SMB

Running Netexec without credentials reveals that we are dealing with a Windows Server 2008, which is quite old

Let’s see if we can enumerate shares using any username

It looks like we can enumerate shares with a guest account, and from the previous output, we can see a non-standard share named ‘Public’. Let’s connect via smbclient and see what files are inside

Inside the Temp directory in the Public share, there is a staff.accdb file that we can download to our local machine to examine it. Running the file command on it reveals that it’s a Microsoft Access database

If we try to open it with Microsoft Access, it prompts us for a password. Luckily, there is an office2john script that we can use to extract the hash and then crack it with John the Ripper

As you can see, john successfully cracked the hash

Now, we can open the database with Microsoft Access and see what’s inside. There is a VBA script, and we can find some credentials for the ‘ldapreader’ user

Bloodhound

With valid credentials in hand, we can run Bloodhound to gain a better understanding of the network and the permissions our user has

Looking for an interesting path to the Domain Controller, we can see the following relationships:

  • The computer Account FS01 is a member of the Domain Computers group.
  • The Domain Computers group has GenericWrite over ADMWS01.
  • ADMWS01 has the AddSelf permission over the Services group.
  • Services group members can RDP to the Domain Controller BLN01.


This is an interesting path! First, we need to gain access to the computer account FS01. So, how are we going to do that?

USER

Pre-Windows 2000 computers

Back in 2022, TrustedSec made a blog post about Pre-Created Computer Accounts that showcased a way to take them over. First, let’s see if that’s the case here using Netexec

As you can see, Netexec shows as the following error message: STATUS_NOLOGON_WORKSTATION_TRUST_ACCOUNT, which means that we have guessed the correct password for a computer account that has not been used yet. Great, now we have found the correct password for FS01. However, we cannot use this computer account yet because the password has not been changed, so let’s do that. We can use this tool by Oddvar Moe called rpcchangepwd

We have successfully changed the FS01 computer account password. We can verify the new credentials using Netexec, which confirms they are valid

GenericWrite

Now that we have control over FS01, we can abuse the GenericWrite permission we identified earlier. The typical techniques to abuse GenericWrite are:

  • shadowCredentials (windows server 2016 or later)
  • targetKerberoasting (the password should be weak enough to be cracked)
  • Resource-Based Constrained Delegation

However, since we are dealing with a Windows Server 2008, none of these techniques will work. So, what we can do in this case? Well, there is another attribute that we can write to, which is unicodePwd. This will allow us reset the password of “ADMWS01$”. To do this, We are going to use the following command:

We didn’t get any error messages from the previous output, so that should have worked successfully. However, We can still verify with Netexec

It looks like the password has been successfully changed.

AddMember

At this stage, we have control over the computer account ‘ADMWS01$,’ which has the AddMember permission over the ‘Services’ group. As we saw earlier, members of this group can RDP to the DC


Since we have the credentials of the ldapreader user, we can add him to this group and RDP to the Domain Controller. We could use the net tool, which is used for the administration of Samba and CIFS/SMB clients. However, this time, I am going to use bloodyAD.

Great, it says our user has been added to the Services group. Therefore, we can RDP to the machine and retrieve the user flag

Because who can resist a nostalgic rendezvous with an OS that refuses to call it quits?

ROOT

Searching for a way to escalate our privileges leads us to the following blog posts by itm4n:

  • https://itm4n.github.io/windows-registry-rpceptmapper-eop/
  • https://itm4n.github.io/windows-registry-rpceptmapper-exploit/

which explain how to exploit a no-fix vulnerability in the RpcEptMapper registry key and provide us with a tool called Perfusion that we can run on the target to obtain a system shell

The exploit is successful, and we are SYSTEM 🐱. Let’s grab our root flag

Even though we got a SYSTEM shell by running the exploit, understanding exactly what the exploit did is way more fruitful and fun. As xct wisely says:

entry.title: Reflection - Vulnlab
entry.content:
Reflection is a medium Active Directory chain from Vulnlab, consisting of 3 machines. It involves MSSQL, NTLM relay attacks, reading LAPS password, Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD), and password reuse.

NMAP

DC01

Based on the Nmap scan results, it is evident that this machine is a domain controller, as it has DNS, LDAP, and Kerberos services running. Additionally, there is an MSSQL service running on port 1433, which is particularly noteworthy

MS01

MS01 also has an MSSQL service running on port 1433

WS01

Finally, there’s WS01, which is nearly identical to MS01, except it doesn’t have the MSSQL service running

Enumeration

SMB

I always prefer to start with SMB enumeration. Let’s run Netexec on the three IPs we have

MS01

It appears that MS01 allows guest authentication. If you’re interested in learning more about guest and null sessions, you can read this article

There is a non-standard share named staging. We can connect to it using Impacket’s smbclient and list the files within the staging share

Great! We’ve obtained some database credentials

MSSQL

We can test these credentials on both DC01 and MS01 (using the --local-auth parameter). Netexec confirms a valid login on MS01

Let’s connect to MSSQL using Impacket’s mssqlclient.

NTLMv2 Hash

Since we’re authenticated to MSSQL, we can attempt to obtain the hash of the user running the database by using the xp_dirtree command. We’ll point it to our machine with a UNC path and then try to crack the hash

As you can see, that was successful. However, the hash couldn’t be cracked. So, what can we do in this situation?

NTLM Relaying

Another approach we can try is relaying the NTLM authentication. But first, we need to verify that SMB signing is disabled

Indeed, SMB signing is disabled on all three machines, including the DC. In this case, we can even relay the authentication to the DC and access its shares.
First, let’s set up a relay server using Impacket’s ntlmrelayx

Next, use the same xp_dirtree command that we used earlier.

As you can see, we’ve successfully received the authentication, and it’s indicating that the attack is targeting the domain controller

Since We used the -socks option with ntlmrelayx, We need to add the following entry to our /etc/proxychains4.conf file

Now, using proxychains, we should be able to list the SMB shares on the DC. There’s a share named prod

We can use smbclient to connect to the prod share and download the prod_db.conf file, which provides us with additional credentials, this time for the prod database

Since the prod share was on the DC, we can attempt to authenticate to the MSSQL instance running on the DC

We can perform some MSSQL enumeration to list the databases and tables. The prod database has a table called users, which contains what appear to be credentials for some domain users

To confirm that these are domain user credentials, we can use Netexec. This confirms that these are indeed valid domain user credentials

With valid credentials in hand, we can run Bloodhound to gain a better understanding of the network and the permissions our users have

GenericAll - 1

The user Abbie.Smith has GenericAll over MS01

I’ve already covered how to abuse GenericAll in my blog. One of the first techniques we can use is Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD). Unfortunately, MachineAccountQuota is set to 0. However, we can still perform another attack known as SPN-less RBCD, which I also covered in this article. A third option is to read the laps password if laps is enabled on the target, which is the case here.
To achieve this, we can use the --laps option in Netexec. As you can see, we retrieved the local administrator password immediately

Now, we can connect to MS01 using evil-winrm and grab our first flag

Credential Dumps

Let’s attempt to dump the credentials from MS01 using the --lsa option in Netexec. However, nothing of interest was found

Another option we can try is the --dpapi option, which will dump the DPAPI credentials. It appears that there is a scheduled task being executed as the user Georgia.Price, which reveals her credentials

WS01

GenericAll - 2

Reviewing the privileges of this new user, we can see that she has GenericAll permissions over WS01

We can attempt to read the LAPS password again, this time on WS01 as the Georgia.Price user. Unfortunately, LAPS is not configured on WS01. In this situation, we can exploit Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) since we already own a machine (MS01), allowing us to use it to carry out our attack
To obtain the machine account hash, we can use Impacket’s secretsdump tool

Another way to retrieve the hash is by using Mimikatz. First, let’s disable Windows Defender and upload Mimikatz

Now, we can run Mimikatz with the following command to dump the machine account hash

Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD)

I’ve already covered this attack in a previous article, or you can check out this excellent article
We can read the msDs-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute, but it’s currently empty.

Now, We want to write this attribute using Impacket’s rbcd tool.

Next, we need to request a service ticket while impersonating the Administrator user

Finally, We can use this ticket to authenticate to WS01. which, as you can see, is successful

Credential Dumps

Just like with MS01, we can dump the LSA secrets from WS01, which reveals the credentials for a new domain user named Rhys.Garner

With this new password, we can perform a credential spraying attack to check for any password reuse. First, let’s dump all the domain users

We do a little bit of cleaning

DC01

Next, we perform the password spraying. Fortunately, the Rhys.Garner user has reused his password with another account named dom_rgarner

The latter is a domain admin. We can login via winrm or directly read the flag using Netexec

That concludes this chain. I hope you learned something new! 🐱

It looks like we got some usernames. Let’s save the output to a file and extract the usernames:

Another thing to try is spraying the usernames as passwords. Maybe some users are using their username as a password:

In this case, they are all guest accounts, so that won’t get us anywhere. Let’s connect to the Public share we saw before using smbclient from impacket:

As you can see, there is a an email message file. We can download it to our machine using the get command, then view it using an online .eml viewer for example. It has a PDF file attached, so let’s download it:

Looking at the JSON output of the spider_plus module, we find many PDFs, but there is a is an interesting file under the IT folder with the .hc extension, which is a VeraCrypt file:

We also see a VeraCrypt installer for ubuntu:

Let’s connect to that share and download the file:

Now, we need a wordlist to use. Thankfully, there is a hint that tells us the format of the password:

Should you need to crack a hash, use a short custom wordlist based on company name & simple mutation rules commonly seen in real life passwords (e.g. year & a special character).

We can quickly make a wordlist based on that and run the hashcat command

After a little bit of time, hashcat was able to crack the file. It is also possible to pass the .hc file directly to hashcat like this:

At this stage, we can open the file in veracrypt and mount it.
As you can see, there are some backups and logs:

We can do a recursive grep for the word “password” but we don’t get any hits. There is a .tar.gz file which is a VyOS backup, let’s extract it and do the recursive grep again:

We got the user lstanley’s password. Again, let’s do a password spray:

We got a hit for the user svc_sspr. Let’s check if that account works with WinRM:

It says (Pwn3d!), so we can connect via evil-winrm:

And grab the user flag:

Privilege Escalation

Bloodhound

Let’s use bloodhound to get a better view of the network and what permissions our user has:

After loading the data in bloodhound and marking our user as owned, we can click on the “First Degree Object Control”

ForceChangePassword

As you can see, the user “svc_sspr” has ForceChangePassword over the users crose, wsilva and rinchols. This means that the user svc_sspr has the capability to change any of these three users’ passwords without knowing their current passwords.

To abuse this we can use the following command, I’ll change wsilva’s password but we can choose any other user, it doesn’t matter:

If we don’t get any errors, it means the password has been successfully changed. We can confirm this by trying to authenticate with the new password:

As you can see, we can successfully authenticate. Now that we have access as the wsilva user, let’s see if he has any interesting permissions.

SPN-less RBCD

Looking at the “outbound object control”, specifically the group delegated object control, we can see an interesting permission:

Basically, wsilva is a member of the ICT SECURITY group, which can modify the msds-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute on the computer. Therefore, we can perform an RBCD (Resource-Based Constrained Delegation) attack.
For this attack to work, the attacker needs to populate the target attribute with the SID of an account that Kerberos can consider as a service. A service ticket will be asked for it. In short, the account must be either:

  • a user account having a ServicePrincipalName set
  • an account with a trailing $ in the sAMAccountName (i.e. a computer accounts)
  • any other account and conduct SPN-less RBCD with U2U (User-to-User) authentication

The common way to conduct these attacks is to create a computer account. This is usually possible thanks to a domain-level attribute called MachineAccountQuota that allows regular users to create up to 10 computer accounts.

Let’s start by enumerating the MachineAccountQuota. We can use the maq module in NetExec:


MachineAccountQuota is 0! How can we perform the RBCD account then? If we do some research, we find this article by Jame Forshaw, which explains how to exploit RBCD using a normal user account. What’s great about this technique is that it allows to abuse RBCD even if the MachineAccountQuota is set to 0. The Hacker Recipes provides an excellent explanation of the steps we need to perform RBCD on SPN-less users.
First, we do the normal RBCD, and instead of a passing a machine account in the -delegate-from option, we will pass the user wsilva:

Then, we need to obtain a TGT through overpass-the-hash to use RC4:

Next, we obtain the TGT session key:

Then, we change the user wsilva’s NT hash with the TGT session key:

The last step is to obtain the delegated service ticket through S4U2self+U2U, followed by S4U2proxy

As you can see, we successfully got a ticket for the administrator user. At this stage, we can perform a DCSync:

We got the administrator hash:

Let’s use it to connect to WinRM:

And grab the root flag:

That concludes this box. I hope you learned something new! 🐱

entry.title: Escape - Vulnlab
entry.content:
Escape is an easy Windows machine created by xct and kozie. It involves Kiosk escape, capturing a password from an encrypted RDP profile, and bypassing UAC.

NMAP

From the NMAP scan, we see just one port open, which is RDP.

RDP

We don’t have any credentials, but we can try to RDP without providing anything and by disabling nla protocol security:

We are presented with a conference display screen and a message saying we can login as KioskUser0 without a password:

Indeed, we got in and find ourselves inside a kiosk mode, a feature used to limit what a user can do on a machine.

Kiosk Escape

So our goal is to escape this mode and get full access to the machine. If we search for kiosk mode escape, we can find this article that talks about it.
An easy way to escape is to press the Windows key, search for msedge and start it, then from the search bar we can type file:///C:/ and go into the C drive

Now, we can navigate to C:/Windows/System32/, click on cmd.exe, and it will download.

After that, we can open the Downloads folder and find it there. However, if we try to open it, the following message appears: This operation has been canceled due to system limitations. Contact your system administrator.

This restriction is due to Kiosk mode, which only allows Microsoft edge. So, what if we rename cmd.exe to msedge

You guessed it right! it will launch cmd.exe. That’s because AppLocker is only checking the file name instead of the path.

User

Now that we’ve escaped the Kiosk mode and have command prompt running, we can grab our user flag.

As you can see, the command prompt is throwing errors. To get rid of that, we can spawn PowerShell, and all those errors would disappear.

PrivEsc

In C:\, we can see a folder called _admin :

Inside it, we find a file called profile.xml related to Remote Desktop Plus.

We can find the actual Remote Desktop Plus program inside C:\Program Files (x86)\Remote Desktop Plus.

Let’s start Remote Desktop Plus and load the profile.xml file inside it by going to Manage profiles -> Import and export -> Import profiles. You’ll need to place the profile.xml file in the Downloads folder since that’s the only location from which we can load files. Now, we can capture the password from memory using a tool called BulletsPassView. We just need to start the tool when the profile gets loaded into the RDP program, and it will immediately find the password, as shown here:

This is the password of the admin user, who is in the Administrators group.

Now that we have the password, we can use runas to spawn a command prompt as the admin user:

UAC Bypass

Although the use is in the Administrators group, he doesn’t have any privileges and that’s because of UAC

To bypass UAC, we can use RunasCs.exe with the --bypass-uac flag:

As you can see, we got a shell as the admin user with all privileges:

Now we can grab the root flag:

That concludes this box. I hope you learned something new! 🐱

entry.title: Sendai - Vulnlab
entry.content:
Sendai is a medium Active Directory machine from Vulnlab, created by xct. This box is a retiring hiring challenge offering multiple paths for exploitation. The path I’ve taken involves resetting a user password with STATUS_PASSWORD_MUST_CHANGE status, abusing GenericALL permissions, and reading the gMSA password. For privilege escalation, we exploit both ESC4 and ESC1.

NMAP

From the Nmap scan, we can see that we are dealing with a Domain Controller, as indicated by the presence of DNS, Kerberos and LDAP.

SMB

Let’s start by enumerating SMB using CrackMapExec

As shown, we can list shares with any user we enter and a null password. Let’s try to get a list of usernames using the --rid-brute flag

That worked, and we successfully got a list of all the users in the domain. Let’s get just the users and put them in a new file

We can attempt to spray a null password with this list of usernames

Password Change

We notice something interesting, the users Elliot and Thomas both have STATUS_PASSWORD_MUST_CHANGE. A quick google search led us to this post here that explains how to reset the password Resetting an Expired Password Remotely. I also found this writeup very helpful Pretending to Be smbpasswd with impacket because we can just use impacket-smbpasswd and set the new password. For this, we can use the following command:

Here, I set the password Passw0rd@ for the user Elliot.Yates. If it asks for the current SMB password we can just press enter for a blank password. Now that we successfully reset Elliot’s password, we can enumerate further

Elliot has read and write access to the config share, let’s use smbclient to connect and explore it

Great, we obtained the MSSQL credentials for the user sqlsvc. However, from the Nmap scan, we don’t see MSSQL

GenericALL

Let’s use bloodhound to get a better view of the network and what permissions our user has. I prefer to use BloodHound from CrackMapExec since it was integrated

From BloodHound we can see that our user Elliot is a member of the Support group, which has GenericAll privileges to the OU ADMSVC@SENDAI.VL. So We can simply add our user to the ADMSVC group

gMSA Password

Now that we are a member of the ADMSVC group, we can retrieve the password for the GMSA MGTSVC, since MGTSVC is a Group Managed Service Account (the path is shown in BloodHound).
To do this, let’s use the --gmsa option in CrackMapExec

Indeed, we were able to retrieve the NTLM of the mgtsvc$ account. Another tool we can use to get the gMSA password is gMSADumper

Now that we have the NTLM hash, let’s connect via winrm

We have obtained the user flag 🚩🐈

PrivEsc

Let’s start our enumeration by running the PrivescCheck.ps1 script

It discovered the credentials of the user clifford.davey

ADCS

Next, let’s do some ADCS enumeration using the ADCS module from CrackMapExec

As observed, ADCS is being utilized on the machine. We can then use Certipy with the find command to identify templates

ESC4

From the Certipy output, we can see that the SendaiComputer template is vulnerable to ESC4. We can refer to this HackTricks article Vulnerable Certificate Template Access Control - ESC4 or this YouTube video AD CS ESC4 Privilege Escalation Tutorial which explains how to abuse ESC4.

Abuse

The first step is to make the certificate vulnerable to ESC1

Now, if we run the Certipy find command again, it will indicate that the template is vulnerable to ESC1. ESC2, ESC3 and ESC4

ESC1

That was successful, we got the administrator.pfx file, which we can use to obtain a TGT and the NTLM hash for the administrator user

With the NTLM hash for the administrator, we will connect over winrm and grab the root flag 🚩🐈

That concludes this box. I hope you learned something new! 🐱
